**Kashinka Hollow** is a tributary of East Branch Briar Creek in Columbia County, Pennsylvania, in the United States. It is approximately 3.0 miles (4.8 km) long and flows through Briar Creek Township.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashinka_Hollow#cite_note-nationalmap-1) Its watershed has an area of 2.08 square miles (5.4 km 2). The median pH of the stream is 7.565. It has the lowest visual assessment score of any stream in the Briar Creek watershed. The stream's watershed lies over limestone, shale, siltstone, and mudstone.
Trout inhabit Kashinka Hollow.

Kashinka Hollow begins half a mile northwest of the community of Summer Hill in Briar Creek Township. It flows west for several tenths of a mile before turning south and flowing into a valley for more than a mile. In the valley, the stream flows parallel to Kachinka Hollow Road. Upon exiting the valley, it continues south for a short distance before turning southwest near Martzville. The stream then turns south again and shortly afterwards reaches its confluence with East Branch Briar Creek.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashinka_Hollow#cite_note-nationalmap-1)
Kashinka Hollow joins East Branch Briar Creek 3.58 miles (5.76 km) upstream of its mouth.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashinka_Hollow#cite_note-gaz-2)
The discharge of Kashinka Hollow ranges from 0.12 to 41.2 cubic feet per second. The median discharge is 2.325 cubic feet per second. The water temperature of the stream ranges from 34.52 to 85.10°F (1.40 to 29.50°C), with a median of 57.02°F (13.90°C). The stream's highest temperature is the highest recorded water temperature of any stream in the watershed of Briar Creek. The electric conductance of the stream's waters ranges from 88 to 301 milli-siemens, with a median of 147 milli-siemens.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashinka_Hollow#cite_note-conservation_plan-3)
The pH of Kashinka Hollow ranges between 7.14 and 8.73. The median pH of the stream is 7.565. The minimum concentration of total dissolved solids is 34 parts per million and the maximum concentration is 86 parts per million. The median concentration is 43.5 parts per million.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashinka_Hollow#cite_note-conservation_plan-3)

In a visual assessment by the Briar Creek Association for Watershed Solutions, Kashinka Hollow was given a score of 3.4 (the lowest in the Briar Creek watershed) on a scale of 1 to 10. It scored best (10 on a scale of 1 to 10) on fish barriers and it scored worst (1 on a scale of 1 to 10) on streambank stability, riparian buffering, and canopy coverage. Of ten sites in the Briar Creek watershed, this location has a priority rank of 1.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashinka_Hollow#cite_note-conservation_plan-3)
Kashinka Hollow sometimes has high levels of lead and nitrates.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashinka_Hollow#cite_note-conservation_plan-3)

## Geography and geology
[edit]
The mouth of Kashinka Hollow has an elevation of 560 to 580 feet (170 to 180 m) above sea level. The source of the stream has an elevation of 980 to 1,000 feet (300 to 300 m) above sea level.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashinka_Hollow#cite_note-nationalmap-1)
The mouth of Kashinka Hollow lies over limestone, while the rest of the watershed's lower reaches lie on shale. Most of the watershed's middle and upper reaches lie over siltstone, but the uppermost reaches are on mudstone.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashinka_Hollow#cite_note-conservation_plan-3)
The soil at one location on Kashinka Hollow is of the Watson Series. This soil series is a fairly well-drained and acidic siltloam. A number of other types of soil are also found in the stream's watershed.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashinka_Hollow#cite_note-conservation_plan-3)
The watershed of Kashinka Hollow has an area of 2.08 square miles (5.4 km 2).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashinka_Hollow#cite_note-gaz-2) The watershed is entirely in Briar Creek Township. Major roads in the stream's watershed include Evansville Road, Summer Hill Road, and Twin Church Road.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashinka_Hollow#cite_note-conservation_plan-3)
Trout reproduce naturally along the entire length of Kashinka Hollow.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashinka_Hollow#cite_note-4)
The Run for the Diamonds passes through Kashinka Hollow.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashinka_Hollow#cite_note-5)

The water in Kashinka Hollow has a median pH of 7.565. This means it's slightly alkaline, or basic. The stream's watershed sits on different types of rock. These include limestone, shale, siltstone, and mudstone. Trout live and reproduce naturally in Kashinka Hollow.

## Stream's Path
Kashinka Hollow starts near a place called Summer Hill. It begins about half a mile northwest of this community. First, it flows west for a short distance. Then, it turns south and enters a valley. It flows through this valley for over a mile.
While in the valley, the stream flows next to Kachinka Hollow Road. After leaving the valley, it continues south. It then turns southwest near a town called Martzville. Finally, the stream turns south again. Soon after, it meets the East Branch Briar Creek. Kashinka Hollow joins East Branch Briar Creek about 3.58 miles (5.76 km) before the East Branch reaches its own mouth.

## Water Conditions
The amount of water flowing in Kashinka Hollow changes. This flow, called discharge, can be from 0.12 to 41.2 cubic feet per second. The average flow is about 2.325 cubic feet per second.
The water temperature also varies. It can be as cool as 34.52°F (1.40°C) or as warm as 85.10°F (29.50°C). The average temperature is 57.02°F (13.90°C). The highest temperature recorded in Kashinka Hollow is the warmest in the whole Briar Creek watershed.
The pH of the water ranges from 7.14 to 8.73. The average pH is 7.565. This means the water is usually slightly basic. The amount of total dissolved solids (like minerals) in the water ranges from 34 to 86 parts per million. The average is 43.5 parts per million.
Sometimes, the water in Kashinka Hollow can have higher amounts of lead and nitrates.

## Water Conditions
### Stream Health Assessment
A group called the Briar Creek Association for Watershed Solutions checked the health of Kashinka Hollow. They gave it a score of 3.4 out of 10. This was the lowest score in the Briar Creek watershed.
The stream scored best (10 out of 10) for how easily fish could move. It scored lowest (1 out of 10) in a few areas. These included the stability of its streambanks. It also scored low on the plants growing along its banks, called riparian buffers. The amount of tree cover, or canopy, was also low.

## Land and Rocks
The place where Kashinka Hollow meets East Branch Briar Creek is about 560 to 580 feet (170 to 180 m) above sea level. The very start of the stream is higher up. It's about 980 to 1,000 feet (300 to 300 m) above sea level.
The area around the mouth of the stream has limestone rock. The lower parts of the watershed are mostly shale. Most of the middle and upper parts of the watershed have siltstone. The very top parts are on mudstone.
The soil in some areas near Kashinka Hollow is called Watson Series soil. This soil is a type of silt loam. It drains water fairly well and is acidic. Other types of soil are also found in the stream's watershed.

## Kashinka Hollow Watershed
The watershed of Kashinka Hollow covers an area of 2.08 square miles (5.4 km 2). A watershed is all the land where water drains into a particular stream or river. This entire watershed is located within Briar Creek Township.
Some important roads in the stream's watershed include Evansville Road, Summer Hill Road, and Twin Church Road.

## Aquatic Life
Trout are found in Kashinka Hollow. They naturally reproduce along the entire length of the stream. This means they lay eggs and new trout hatch there.

## Fun Activities
The "Run for the Diamonds" is a race that passes through the area of Kashinka Hollow.

Title: Governor Shapiro Calls for the End of the Death Penalty in Pennsylvania
Chunks: 0,1,2
###### May 01, 2023
On February 16, 2023, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro called on the state legislature to abolish the death penalty. He also announced that he will not sign any death warrants as governor, halting executions for state crimes in Pennsylvania during his time in office.
To ensure that executions do not resume after Governor Shapiro’s time in office, both houses of the Pennsylvania legislature would need to vote to abolish the death penalty. One day after Governor Shapiro’s announcement, a bill to abolish the death penalty was introduced in both chambers of the legislature. Democrats have a slight majority in the Pennsylvania House of Representatives, while Republicans occupy 28 of the 50 seats in the Senate.
Governor Shapiro’s position on the death penalty has shifted over time. When he was first elected as Pennsylvania Attorney General in 2016, he was a supporter of the death penalty, but he found himself unable to seek the death penalty when cases came across his desk. He also spoke about the Tree of Life shooting, a 2018 anti-Semitic terrorist attack killing 11 at a synagogue in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Governor Shapiro initially wanted the federal government to seek the death penalty against the perpetrator. However, he listened to many of the Tree of Life victim’s families, who asked him to use his power to discourage the federal government from seeking the death penalty, which led to Governor Shapiro reevaluating his own position on the issue.
Governor Shapiro gave a number of reasons for his decision not to allow executions to go forward while he is governor. He cited the irreversibility and fallibility of the death penalty, as 11 people have been exonerated from death row in Pennsylvania in the modern era of the death penalty. Governor Shapiro also recalled being unable to look his son in the eye and answer his question about why it is fair to kill people as a punishment for killing.
Pennsylvania has a long history with the death penalty. The state executed over 1,000 people before the death penalty was abolished nationwide in 1972, making it the third largest user of capital punishment in that time period. After the United States Supreme Court, in 1976, announced new constitutional requirements for death penalty schemes, Pennsylvania reinstated the death penalty in 1978.

###### May 01, 2023
Since 1978, three people have been executed in Pennsylvania. All three of these individuals were “volunteers”, meaning they voluntarily waived their right to appeal their sentences. In 1990, Justice Thurgood Marshall pointed out that executing a defendant who has not appealed their sentence may lead to an unnecessary risk of the execution of an innocent person, a person who does not deserve the sentence of death, and people who were denied their fundamental rights in the legal system. He furtherwrote, “A defendant's voluntary submission to a barbaric punishment does not ameliorate the harm that imposing such a punishment causes to our basic societal values and to the integrity of our system of justice. Certainly a defendant's consent to being drawn and quartered or burned at the stake would not license the State to exact such punishments.”
Pennsylvania has not carried out an execution since 1999. At the time of a 2022report, there were 128 people on death row in Pennsylvania, making it the 7th largest death row in the United States. The report also found that Pennsylvania had the 6th highest percentage of minorities on death row among U.S. states (with 10 or more people on death row). Over 60% of the people on death row in Pennsylvania are minorities although more than 80% of Pennsylvania’s population is white.
Pennsylvania death penalty experts point to additional concerns regarding the application of the death penalty. Robert Dunham, Senior Policy Analyst and former Executive Director of the Death Penalty Information Center, pointed out that Philadelphia County has had more death sentences overturned due to prosecutorial misconduct than any other county in the United States. Six innocent people have been exonerated from death row whose cases involved police or prosecutorial misconduct. Further, Pennsylvania is the only state to not provide funding for indigent defense at any stage of the capital trial and appeal process, relying instead on a county-by-county system that leads to numerous inequities and inconsistencies in the quality of representation provided to indigent defendants and prisoners. Dunham noted that more than 125 death sentences have been overturned in Pennsylvania due to ineffective assistance of counsel, making it the most common reason to overturn a sentence of death.

###### May 01, 2023
A Death Penalty Information Centerreporthighlighted several defendants whose Pennsylvania death sentences were reversed due to ineffective assistance of counsel. One of these defendants is Henry Fahy, whose trial attorney failed to present mitigating evidence about his extensive history of mental illness and sexual and physical childhood abuse. Another notable case is that of Carolyn King, whose trial attorney was unfamiliar with the basic procedure of capital cases and spent less than an hour and a half preparing for the punishment phase of the trial. King had a long history of abuse, both as a child and as an adult, and met the criteria for several mental illnesses, including depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, and a personality disorder. Nevertheless, her attorney failed to present easily available mitigating evidence of King’s background. Based on the report, failure to develop mitigating evidence was a common basis for courts to find ineffective assistance of counsel.
If Pennsylvania does abolish the death penalty, it will be the24th stateto do so. Currently, Pennsylvania is one of the 14 states where the death penalty is a legal punishment, but an execution has not been carried out within the last 10 years. Pennsylvania is not the only state currently exploring death penalty reform or pausing executions. Like Pennsylvania, Oregon, California, Arizona, and the Federal Government all are under formal death penaltymoratoriums. On April 10, 2023, Louisiana Governor John Bel Edwards also called for the abolition of the state’s death penalty. In December 2022, Oregon Governor Kate Browncommutedall of the state’s 17 death sentences and repurposed Oregon’s execution chambers.Californiais in the process of dismantling its death row. In Arizona, Governor Katie Hobbs ordered anexaminationof the death penalty in Arizona, specifically focusing on potential issues with the state’s two execution methods: lethal injection and the gas chamber. The Arizona Attorney General announced that the state would not push forward execution warrants while the investigation is ongoing. Meanwhile, Texas, Florida, Missouri, and Oklahoma all have executions scheduled in the coming months, including seven more executions scheduled in Oklahoma by the end of 2023.

###### May 01, 2023
On February 16, 2023, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro called on the state legislature to abolish the death penalty. He also announced that he will not sign any death warrants as governor, halting executions for state crimes in Pennsylvania during his time in office.
To ensure that executions do not resume after Governor Shapiro’s time in office, both houses of the Pennsylvania legislature would need to vote to abolish the death penalty. One day after Governor Shapiro’s announcement, a bill to abolish the death penalty was introduced in both chambers of the legislature. Democrats have a slight majority in the Pennsylvania House of Representatives, while Republicans occupy 28 of the 50 seats in the Senate.
Governor Shapiro’s position on the death penalty has shifted over time. When he was first elected as Pennsylvania Attorney General in 2016, he was a supporter of the death penalty, but he found himself unable to seek the death penalty when cases came across his desk. He also spoke about the Tree of Life shooting, a 2018 anti-Semitic terrorist attack killing 11 at a synagogue in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Governor Shapiro initially wanted the federal government to seek the death penalty against the perpetrator. However, he listened to many of the Tree of Life victim’s families, who asked him to use his power to discourage the federal government from seeking the death penalty, which led to Governor Shapiro reevaluating his own position on the issue.
Governor Shapiro gave a number of reasons for his decision not to allow executions to go forward while he is governor. He cited the irreversibility and fallibility of the death penalty, as 11 people have been exonerated from death row in Pennsylvania in the modern era of the death penalty. Governor Shapiro also recalled being unable to look his son in the eye and answer his question about why it is fair to kill people as a punishment for killing.
Pennsylvania has a long history with the death penalty. The state executed over 1,000 people before the death penalty was abolished nationwide in 1972, making it the third largest user of capital punishment in that time period. After the United States Supreme Court, in 1976, announced new constitutional requirements for death penalty schemes, Pennsylvania reinstated the death penalty in 1978.
texts.1:
###### May 01, 2023
Since 1978, three people have been executed in Pennsylvania. All three of these individuals were “volunteers”, meaning they voluntarily waived their right to appeal their sentences. In 1990, Justice Thurgood Marshall pointed out that executing a defendant who has not appealed their sentence may lead to an unnecessary risk of the execution of an innocent person, a person who does not deserve the sentence of death, and people who were denied their fundamental rights in the legal system. He furtherwrote, “A defendant's voluntary submission to a barbaric punishment does not ameliorate the harm that imposing such a punishment causes to our basic societal values and to the integrity of our system of justice. Certainly a defendant's consent to being drawn and quartered or burned at the stake would not license the State to exact such punishments.”
Pennsylvania has not carried out an execution since 1999. At the time of a 2022report, there were 128 people on death row in Pennsylvania, making it the 7th largest death row in the United States. The report also found that Pennsylvania had the 6th highest percentage of minorities on death row among U.S. states (with 10 or more people on death row). Over 60% of the people on death row in Pennsylvania are minorities although more than 80% of Pennsylvania’s population is white.
Pennsylvania death penalty experts point to additional concerns regarding the application of the death penalty. Robert Dunham, Senior Policy Analyst and former Executive Director of the Death Penalty Information Center, pointed out that Philadelphia County has had more death sentences overturned due to prosecutorial misconduct than any other county in the United States. Six innocent people have been exonerated from death row whose cases involved police or prosecutorial misconduct. Further, Pennsylvania is the only state to not provide funding for indigent defense at any stage of the capital trial and appeal process, relying instead on a county-by-county system that leads to numerous inequities and inconsistencies in the quality of representation provided to indigent defendants and prisoners. Dunham noted that more than 125 death sentences have been overturned in Pennsylvania due to ineffective assistance of counsel, making it the most common reason to overturn a sentence of death.
texts.2:
###### May 01, 2023
A Death Penalty Information Centerreporthighlighted several defendants whose Pennsylvania death sentences were reversed due to ineffective assistance of counsel. One of these defendants is Henry Fahy, whose trial attorney failed to present mitigating evidence about his extensive history of mental illness and sexual and physical childhood abuse. Another notable case is that of Carolyn King, whose trial attorney was unfamiliar with the basic procedure of capital cases and spent less than an hour and a half preparing for the punishment phase of the trial. King had a long history of abuse, both as a child and as an adult, and met the criteria for several mental illnesses, including depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, and a personality disorder. Nevertheless, her attorney failed to present easily available mitigating evidence of King’s background. Based on the report, failure to develop mitigating evidence was a common basis for courts to find ineffective assistance of counsel.
If Pennsylvania does abolish the death penalty, it will be the24th stateto do so. Currently, Pennsylvania is one of the 14 states where the death penalty is a legal punishment, but an execution has not been carried out within the last 10 years. Pennsylvania is not the only state currently exploring death penalty reform or pausing executions. Like Pennsylvania, Oregon, California, Arizona, and the Federal Government all are under formal death penaltymoratoriums. On April 10, 2023, Louisiana Governor John Bel Edwards also called for the abolition of the state’s death penalty. In December 2022, Oregon Governor Kate Browncommutedall of the state’s 17 death sentences and repurposed Oregon’s execution chambers.Californiais in the process of dismantling its death row. In Arizona, Governor Katie Hobbs ordered anexaminationof the death penalty in Arizona, specifically focusing on potential issues with the state’s two execution methods: lethal injection and the gas chamber. The Arizona Attorney General announced that the state would not push forward execution warrants while the investigation is ongoing. Meanwhile, Texas, Florida, Missouri, and Oklahoma all have executions scheduled in the coming months, including seven more executions scheduled in Oklahoma by the end of 2023.
